subject: maths
title: Primary 2 Adding and Subtracting Fractions
seo_title: P2 Adding and Subtracting Fractions Worksheets: Free Primary 2 Maths with Answers (MOE Syllabus)
standard_text: Adding and subtracting like fractions within one whole (denominators not exceeding 12)
meta_desc: Free P2 maths practice: add and subtract like fractions with fraction bars, make 1 whole and solve word problems. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: When the denominators are the same, add or subtract only the numerators.
body_html:
Like fractions

Like fractions have the same denominator, such as 27 and 37. The parts are the same size. So we just count the parts.

Adding like fractions

Add the numerators. The denominator stays the same.

Example

27 + 37 = ?

Add the numerators: 2 + 3 = 5. Keep the denominator 7.

Answer: 57

Subtracting like fractions

Subtract the numerators. The denominator stays the same.

Example

79 − 39 = ?

Subtract the numerators: 7 − 3 = 4. Keep the denominator 9.

Answer: 49

Making 1 whole

1 whole has all the parts: 1 = 44 = 88. To make 1, the numerators must add up to the denominator.

Example

38 + ? = 1

1 = 88. 8 − 3 = 5.

Answer: 58

Word problems: draw a model

Draw a bar for the whole. Cut it into equal units. Mark what you know. Put “?” on the part to find.

Example

Ali ate 28 of a pizza. Siti ate 38 of it. How much of the pizza was left?

Eaten: 2 + 3 = 5 units. Left: 8 − 5 = 3 units.

Answer: 38

Common mistakes

MistakeCorrect
15 + 25 = 310 (adding the denominators)Keep the denominator: 35
58 − 28 = 30 (subtracting the denominators)Keep the denominator: 38
1 − 38 = 28 (taking 1 from the numerator)Write 1 as 88: 88 − 38 = 58

faq.q: What is taught in P2 fractions?
faq.a: In Primary 2, students learn halves, thirds, quarters and other unit fractions, compare fractions, and add and subtract like fractions within one whole, such as 2/7 + 3/7 = 5/7.

faq.q: How do I explain adding fractions to my child?
faq.a: Cut a paper strip into equal parts and colour them. 2 fifths and 1 more fifth make 3 fifths, so only the numerator changes: 2/5 + 1/5 = 3/5.

faq.q: What is the most common mistake when adding fractions?
faq.a: Adding the denominators, as in 1/5 + 2/5 = 3/10. The parts are still fifths, so the answer is 3/5.

faq.q: Is adding and subtracting fractions in the MOE syllabus for Primary 2?
faq.a: Yes. Adding and subtracting like fractions within one whole, with denominators up to 12, is part of Fractions in the Primary 2 Standard Mathematics syllabus (MOE 2021). Related fractions and simplest form come in Primary 3.

items.q: Ali and Siti shared a pizza. Ali ate 28 of it (green). Siti ate 38 of it (yellow). How much of the pizza did they eat altogether?

items.q: Mrs Lim cut a pandan cake into 6 equal slices. Her family ate 16 of the cake at lunch. They ate 46 of it at dinner. How much of the cake did they eat?
items.e: The model has 6 units. 1 unit + 4 units = 5 units. The parts are sixths, so the denominator stays 6. Add the numerators: 1 + 4 = 5. The answer is 56.

items.q: Mei Ling drank 15 of her water before recess. She drank 25 of it after recess. How much of her water did she drink?

items.q: Jun Jie and his father painted a fence. They painted 37 of it on Saturday and 47 of it on Sunday. How much of the fence did they paint?
items.e: The parts are sevenths, so the denominator stays 7. Add the numerators: 3 + 4 = 7. 77 is all the parts, so 77 = 1 whole. The answer is 1.

items.q: Raju’s family cut a watermelon into 8 equal slices. They ate 58 of it. How much of the watermelon was left?
items.e: The whole watermelon is 1. Left = 1 − eaten. 1 whole is 88. 88 − 58 = 38.

items.q: Priya had a ribbon. She used 49 of it to make a bow. How much of the ribbon was left?
items.e: The model shows 9 units. 4 units were used, so 9 − 4 = 5 units are left. 1 whole is 99. 99 − 49 = 59.

items.q: A jug was 710 full of soya bean milk. Mdm Wong poured out 410 of the jug. How full is the jug now?
items.e: “Poured out” means take away. The parts are tenths, so the denominator stays 10. Subtract the numerators: 7 − 4 = 3. The answer is 310.

items.q: Ahmad ate 712 of a pizza. Nurul ate 212 of the same pizza. How much more did Ahmad eat than Nurul?
items.e: “How much more” means subtract. The difference is 5 units. The parts are twelfths, so the denominator stays 12. Subtract the numerators: 7 − 2 = 5. The answer is 512.

items.q: Xin Yi read 311 of a library book on Monday. She read 511 of it on Tuesday. How much of the book did she read on the two days?

items.q: Hafiz has read 29 of his storybook. How much of the book has he not read yet?

items.q: Chloe ate 29 of a cake. Ryan ate 39 of the cake. How much of the cake was left?
items.e: The model has 9 units. Chloe and Ryan ate 2 + 3 = 5 units. 9 − 5 = 4 units are left. So 99 − 59 = 49 of the cake is left.

items.q: Class 2A visited Gardens by the Bay. They walked 49 of a trail before lunch and 39 of it after lunch. How much of the trail did they still have to walk?
items.e: The model has 9 units. The class walked 4 + 3 = 7 units. 9 − 7 = 2 units are still to walk. The answer is 29.

items.q: Nurul and Farah shared a pizza. They ate the whole pizza. Nurul ate 38 of it. How much of the pizza did Farah eat?
items.e: The whole pizza is 1. Farah ate 1 − 38. 1 whole is 88. 88 − 38 = 58.
